newsitem.title: USA: Wind shift helps battle against California blazes.
newsitem.headline: Wind shift helps battle against California blazes.

text.p: Fierce hot winds that fuelled a rash of wildfires in tinder-dry southern California died down on Wednesday, allowing firefighters to gain the upper hand.

Weather forecasters said the Santa Ana winds, which had roared across the region at more than 50 mph (80 kph), fell to 15 mph (25 kph) and would disappear later in the day. Humidity rose as sea breezes took over.
However, meteorologists predicted that the Santa Ana winds could return again at the weekend, raising fears of renewed fires.

The wind-blown wildfires erupted Monday from the movie star colony of Malibu to mountains along the Mexican border. They have destroyed or damaged more than 100 homes, injured 11 people and burned some 35,000 acres (14,000 hectares) of land.
Firefighters said the blaze in Malibu, which burned nearly 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares), was 33 percent contained and they were in control of the other fires despite isolated hot-spots.
One fireman was fighting for his life after he and five colleagues were trapped in their firetruck when a wall of flames jumped a road in a canyon north of Los Angeles.
The man was listed in critical condition in the hospital with life-threatening injuries -- burns over 60 percent of his body and respiratory problems.
"Two rigs were out on the road and one of them stalled. They were engulfed and got burned, they couldn't get out," said Don Wittey of the Los Angeles Fire Department.
In the Santa Monica hills overlooking Malibu, some residents returned to their homes amid charred tree trunks and scorched brush.
Oliver Bendig was one of the unlucky ones, who found only smouldering ruins. "It was a beautiful home -- it's gone," he said, surveying the smoking debris. "It had windows, windows all around."
Another resident, Lloyd Smith, tried to salvage what he could from the ruins of his family house built 50 years ago.
"When I was growing up, I helped my dad build extensions," he said, adding that his $50,000 record collection had gone up in smoke.

California Governor Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency in San Diego, Los Angeles and Orange Counties on Tuesday and sent a letter to President Bill Clinton seeking to classify the fire-ravaged areas as major disaster areas, making them eligible for federal funds.
